question: How did my phone-drawer focus plan change?

retrieval.warning: Exact quotations prove provenance, not semantic support.

evidence.title: 2026-06-10-focus-plan
evidence.quote:
# Focus plan, June 10

I thought putting my phone in a drawer would solve most of my study interruptions. My initial plan was to do a 25-minute work block with the phone out of reach, then take a five-minute break. I tried this for three morning sessions. I wrote down fewer phone checks in those sessions, but I did not measure total work completed or compare the sessions with a similar week. This note records an attempt and an early interpretation, not evidence that the phone was the main cause of lost time.

The biggest unresolved question was what happened when I sat down without a clear next action. I sometimes spent the first ten minutes deciding which problem to start. I planned to test that separately. A later note, `life-focus-correction-2026-07-04`, revises my explanation; the drawer plan remains here as history.

evidence.title: 2026-07-04-focus-correction
evidence.quote:
# Correction: starting friction, July 4

I revisited the June phone-drawer idea after four library sessions. On two days I hid the phone but still lost time deciding what to do. On the other two days I wrote a single next action before the session, such as “solve question 3 without notes,” and began sooner even though the phone stayed on the desk. These are informal observations with several changing conditions; they do not prove that next-action planning caused the improvement.

My corrected working belief is that an unclear first task may have mattered more than access to the phone in this small set of sessions. I no longer describe the drawer as the complete solution. I want to combine a written next action with reduced notifications, then compare several sessions using the same start-time measure. The older note is superseded as advice but should remain readable as the original attempt.

evidence.title: 2026-07-18-focus-decision
evidence.quote:
# Next focus experiment, July 18

For the next two weeks, I will write the first concrete action on a card before each morning work block, silence notifications for 30 minutes, and log the minutes from sitting down to starting that action. I will compare those logs with my previous sessions, while treating the comparison as informal because task difficulty and location may differ.

This is a decision and a measurement plan, not a completed experiment. I have not recorded the two-week results here. If the logs show little change or the routine is too annoying to keep, I will stop recommending it as my default. This decision draws on the July 4 correction, which superseded my June phone-only explanation.

answer: On June 10, the user tried a phone-drawer plan to reduce study interruptions, noting fewer checks but no measurement of work output [E1]. By July 4, they revised their working belief, noting that unclear first tasks caused delays even when the phone was hidden, so the drawer alone was not the complete solution [E2]. On July 18, they planned a new experiment combining a written next action with silenced notifications, treating the comparison to earlier sessions as informal [E3].

claims.text: The June 10 note records an attempt to reduce interruptions with a phone drawer, observing fewer checks but no work-output comparison [E1].
The July 4 correction revises the working belief that an unclear first task may have mattered more than phone access in the small session set [E2].
The July 18 note plans a new experiment combining a written next action with silenced notifications, comparing logs informally to prior sessions [E3].

limitations: No evidence establishes that the phone drawer caused measurable changes in work completed.
The July 4 and July 18 notes involve multiple changing conditions, so no single factor is proven causal.
The July 18 experiment has not been run; results are not yet available.
